lessons.title: Cell Structure
lessons.content: All living things are made of cells. Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts (for photosynthesis), and a large central vacuole. Animal cells lack these but share organelles: the nucleus (contains DNA), mitochondria (produce energy), ribosomes (make proteins), endoplasmic reticulum (transport), and cell membrane (controls entry/exit). Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) are simpler with no nucleus. Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals) have a defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
examples: Red blood cells lack a nucleus to carry more haemoglobin
Plant cells are rigid (cell wall); animal cells are flexible
Mitochondria are the 'powerhouse' — they produce ATP

keyTerms.cell membrane: Selectively permeable barrier surrounding the cell
keyTerms.chloroplast: Organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis occurs

quiz.question: Which organelle is in plant cells but NOT animal cells?
quiz.explanation: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis — only in plant cells.

quiz.question: Function of mitochondria?
quiz.explanation: Mitochondria break down glucose to produce ATP energy.

quiz.question: Bacteria are:
quiz.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes — no membrane-bound nucleus.

quiz.question: Which organelle makes proteins?
quiz.explanation: Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis in all cells.

quiz.question: The cell membrane is described as:
quiz.explanation: It allows some substances through while blocking others.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration
lessons.content: Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Happens in chloroplasts using chlorophyll. Cellular respiration is the reverse — cells break down glucose to release energy: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen. Anaerobic works without oxygen, producing lactic acid (animals) or ethanol (yeast) but less energy.
examples: Leaves are green because chlorophyll reflects green light
You breathe faster during exercise — muscles need more O₂ for respiration
Bread rises — yeast produces CO₂ through anaerobic respiration

keyTerms.photosynthesis: Plants convert light energy, CO₂, and water into glucose and O₂
keyTerms.cellular respiration: Breaking down glucose to release energy (ATP)
keyTerms.chlorophyll: Green pigment absorbing light for photosynthesis
keyTerms.anaerobic: Without oxygen — produces less energy plus lactic acid or ethanol

quiz.question: Plants absorb which gas for photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: Plants take in CO₂ and release O₂.

quiz.question: Where does photosynthesis occur?
quiz.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll — the site of photosynthesis.

quiz.question: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces:
quiz.explanation: Yeast fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

quiz.question: What factors affect the rate of photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: All three are limiting factors — increase any one to speed up photosynthesis.

quiz.question: Respiration occurs in:
quiz.explanation: Every living cell respires — it's how all organisms release energy from food.

lessons.title: Cell Division
lessons.content: Cells divide to grow and repair. Mitosis produces two identical cells — DNA copies, then the cell splits. Meiosis produces four cells with half the chromosomes (gametes). Cancer occurs when cell division becomes uncontrolled. The cell cycle: G1 (growth), S (DNA copies), G2 (preparation), M (mitosis). Stem cells are unspecialised — they can become any cell type.
examples: Skin cells divide by mitosis every 2-3 weeks
Humans: 46 chromosomes; gametes have 23 each
Stem cells can develop into blood cells, nerve cells, muscle cells — any type needed

keyTerms.mitosis: Division producing two identical daughter cells
keyTerms.meiosis: Division producing four gametes with half the chromosomes
keyTerms.stem cells: Unspecialised cells that can develop into different cell types
keyTerms.cell cycle: The stages a cell goes through including growth and division

quiz.question: Mitosis produces:
quiz.explanation: Mitosis = two genetically identical daughter cells.

quiz.question: Gametes are produced by:
quiz.explanation: Meiosis halves chromosomes for sex cells.

quiz.question: Human body cells have:
quiz.explanation: 23 pairs = 46 chromosomes in body cells.

quiz.question: Cancer is caused by:
quiz.explanation: Mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle cause uncontrolled growth.

quiz.question: Stem cells are special because:
options: They can become any cell type
quiz.explanation: Stem cells are unspecialised and can differentiate into various cell types.

lessons.title: Transport Across Membranes
lessons.content: Substances move in and out of cells through the cell membrane. Diffusion: particles move from high concentration to low concentration — no energy needed (passive). Examples: oxygen diffusing into blood in the lungs, CO₂ diffusing out. Osmosis: the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution. Active transport: moving substances against the concentration gradient (low to high) — requires energy from ATP. Examples: root hair cells absorbing minerals from soil, glucose absorption in the gut.
examples: Diffusion: perfume spreading across a room from high concentration to low
Osmosis: plant roots absorbing water from moist soil — water moves into the more concentrated cell sap
Active transport: root hair cells use energy to absorb nitrate ions even when soil concentration is lower than inside the cell

keyTerms.diffusion: Net movement of particles from high to low concentration — passive, no energy
keyTerms.osmosis: Diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane
keyTerms.active transport: Moving substances against the concentration gradient — requires ATP energy
keyTerms.concentration gradient: The difference in concentration between two areas

quiz.question: Diffusion is movement from:
quiz.explanation: Diffusion is passive — particles naturally move from high to low concentration.

quiz.question: Osmosis involves the movement of:
quiz.explanation: Osmosis is specifically the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.

quiz.question: Active transport requires:
quiz.explanation: Active transport moves substances against the gradient — this requires energy.

quiz.question: A red blood cell in pure water would:
options: Swell and burst (water enters by osmosis)
quiz.explanation: Pure water is more dilute than the cell — water enters by osmosis, causing the cell to swell and burst.

quiz.question: Which is NOT an example of diffusion?
options: Root cells absorbing minerals using ATP
Oxygen entering blood in the lungs
quiz.explanation: Mineral absorption against the gradient uses active transport, not diffusion.

lessons.title: Enzymes
lessons.content: Enzymes are biological catalysts — proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being used up. Each enzyme has a specific shape (active site) that fits only certain substrates — the lock and key model. Factors affecting enzyme activity: temperature (too high denatures the enzyme — its shape changes permanently), pH (each enzyme has an optimum pH), and substrate concentration. Enzymes in digestion: amylase breaks starch into sugars, protease breaks proteins into amino acids, lipase breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Enzymes work best at body temperature (~37°C) and specific pH values.
examples: Amylase in saliva starts digesting starch in your mouth — that's why chewing a cracker makes it taste sweet
Pepsin in the stomach works at pH 2 (acidic) — it would stop working in the alkaline small intestine
Biological washing powders contain enzymes (proteases, lipases) to break down stains at low temperatures

keyTerms.enzyme: A biological catalyst that speeds up reactions without being consumed
keyTerms.active site: The specific region of an enzyme where the substrate binds
keyTerms.denature: When an enzyme's shape is permanently changed (by heat or extreme pH), losing function
keyTerms.substrate: The molecule that an enzyme acts upon

quiz.question: Enzymes are:
quiz.explanation: Enzymes are proteins that speed up biochemical reactions.

quiz.question: At very high temperatures, enzymes:
options: Denature — their shape changes and they stop working
quiz.explanation: Heat above the optimum permanently changes the enzyme's active site shape.

quiz.question: The lock and key model describes:
options: How an enzyme's active site fits a specific substrate
quiz.explanation: The substrate (key) fits precisely into the enzyme's active site (lock).

quiz.question: Amylase breaks down:
quiz.explanation: Amylase is the enzyme specific to starch digestion.

quiz.question: Biological washing powders work at low temperatures because:
options: They contain enzymes that break down stains
quiz.explanation: Enzymes in bio-powders digest protein and fat stains even in cool water.

lessons.title: Digestive System
lessons.content: Digestion breaks food into absorbable nutrients. Mouth: teeth chew, saliva has amylase (starch). Oesophagus: peristalsis pushes food down. Stomach: HCl acid + pepsin digest proteins. Small intestine: most absorption via villi (huge surface area). Liver produces bile (emulsifies fats). Pancreas releases enzymes. Large intestine absorbs water. Waste exits as faeces.
examples: Chewing a cracker for 30s makes it sweet — amylase breaks starch to sugar
Small intestine is ~6m long for massive absorption surface
Bile breaks fat droplets into tiny ones for easier enzyme action

keyTerms.peristalsis: Wave-like muscle contractions pushing food through the tract
keyTerms.villi: Finger-like projections increasing absorption surface area
keyTerms.bile: Liver product that emulsifies fats into smaller droplets

quiz.question: Where does most nutrient absorption occur?
quiz.explanation: Villi in the small intestine absorb nutrients into blood.

quiz.question: Bile does what?
quiz.explanation: Bile breaks large fat globules into smaller droplets.

quiz.question: Amylase breaks down:
quiz.explanation: Amylase converts starch into sugars.

quiz.question: Villi increase surface area for:
quiz.explanation: More surface area = more efficient absorption of digested nutrients.

quiz.question: The large intestine mainly absorbs:
quiz.explanation: The large intestine absorbs water from undigested food, forming solid waste.

lessons.title: Circulatory System
lessons.content: The heart pumps blood. Four chambers: right atrium/ventricle (pump to lungs), left atrium/ventricle (pump to body). Arteries carry blood away from heart (thick walls, high pressure). Veins carry blood back (thin walls, valves). Capillaries: tiny vessels for exchange. Red blood cells carry O₂ using haemoglobin. White blood cells fight infections. Platelets help clotting. Double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice per circuit (heart→lungs→heart→body→heart).
examples: Heart beats ~100,000 times per day
Arteries have thick muscular walls for high pressure
Cut yourself: platelets form a clot to stop bleeding

keyTerms.artery: Vessel carrying blood away from heart
keyTerms.vein: Vessel carrying blood back to heart
keyTerms.haemoglobin: Protein in red blood cells carrying oxygen
keyTerms.double circulation: Blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit

quiz.question: Which chamber pumps blood to the body?
quiz.explanation: Left ventricle has the thickest wall — pumps oxygenated blood to the body.

quiz.question: Oxygen is carried by:
quiz.explanation: Haemoglobin binds oxygen for transport.

quiz.question: Veins have valves to:
quiz.explanation: Valves ensure one-way flow back to the heart.

quiz.question: Where does gas exchange occur?
quiz.explanation: Capillary walls are one cell thick — O₂ and CO₂ diffuse through.

quiz.question: Double circulation means:
options: Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit
quiz.explanation: Heart→lungs→heart→body→heart. Two passes through the heart per circuit.

lessons.title: Respiratory System
lessons.content: The respiratory system gets oxygen into the blood and removes carbon dioxide. Air enters through the nose/mouth, passes through the trachea (windpipe), which splits into two bronchi (one to each lung), then smaller bronchioles, ending in tiny air sacs called alveoli. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli: oxygen diffuses from air into blood capillaries; CO₂ diffuses from blood into the alveoli to be breathed out. Alveoli are adapted for efficient exchange: enormous surface area (~70 m²), walls one cell thick, moist surfaces, and rich blood supply. Breathing is controlled by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.
examples: You have about 300 million alveoli — giving a tennis-court-sized surface area for gas exchange
Breathing in: diaphragm contracts (flattens), ribcage rises, lung volume increases, air rushes in
Smoking damages alveoli (emphysema) — reduced surface area means less oxygen absorption

keyTerms.alveoli: Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs
keyTerms.gas exchange: Oxygen diffusing into blood and CO₂ diffusing out in the alveoli
keyTerms.diaphragm: A dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that controls breathing
keyTerms.trachea: The windpipe — carries air from the throat to the bronchi

quiz.question: Gas exchange occurs in:
quiz.explanation: Alveoli are the tiny air sacs where O₂ and CO₂ are exchanged.

quiz.question: Alveoli walls are:
options: One cell thick for easy diffusion
quiz.explanation: Thin walls minimise diffusion distance for efficient gas exchange.

quiz.question: When you breathe in, the diaphragm:
quiz.explanation: Diaphragm contracts (flattens) → lung volume increases → air pressure drops → air flows in.

quiz.question: The total surface area of alveoli is approximately:
quiz.explanation: 300 million tiny alveoli create ~70 m² of surface area — incredibly efficient.

quiz.question: Smoking damages the respiratory system by:
options: Destroying alveoli and reducing surface area for gas exchange
quiz.explanation: Tar and toxins destroy alveoli (emphysema), reducing the area available for gas exchange.

lessons.title: Nervous System
lessons.content: The nervous system coordinates the body using electrical signals. CNS = brain + spinal cord. Peripheral nervous system connects CNS to the body. Neurons: sensory (receptors → CNS), relay (within CNS), motor (CNS → muscles). Reflex arc: stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector. Reflexes bypass the brain for speed. Synapses are gaps between neurons — chemicals (neurotransmitters) cross them.
examples: Touching hot stove: reflex — hand moves before you feel pain
Brain regions: cerebrum (thinking), cerebellum (balance), medulla (breathing)
Nerve impulses travel at up to 120 m/s

keyTerms.neuron: A nerve cell transmitting electrical signals
keyTerms.reflex arc: Automatic rapid pathway bypassing the brain
keyTerms.synapse: Gap between neurons where chemical signals cross
keyTerms.neurotransmitter: Chemical released at a synapse to transmit the signal to the next neuron

quiz.question: Sensory neurons carry signals:
quiz.explanation: Sensory neurons detect stimuli and carry signals to the brain/spinal cord.

quiz.question: Reflexes are fast because:
quiz.explanation: Reflex arcs go through the spinal cord — faster than processing in the brain.

quiz.question: The CNS consists of:
quiz.explanation: Central Nervous System = brain + spinal cord.

quiz.question: At a synapse, the signal crosses as:
quiz.explanation: Neurotransmitters (chemicals) diffuse across the synaptic gap to the next neuron.

quiz.question: The cerebellum controls:
quiz.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

lessons.title: Hormones and the Endocrine System
lessons.content: The endocrine system uses hormones (chemical messengers) transported in blood to target organs. Unlike the nervous system (fast, short-lived, electrical), hormones are slower but have longer-lasting effects. Key glands: pituitary (master gland — controls others), thyroid (metabolism rate), adrenal (adrenaline for fight-or-flight), pancreas (insulin and glucagon for blood sugar), ovaries (oestrogen), testes (testosterone). Blood sugar regulation: after eating, blood glucose rises → pancreas releases insulin → cells absorb glucose → level drops. In diabetes, this system fails — Type 1: no insulin produced; Type 2: cells don't respond to insulin.
examples: Adrenaline: heart rate increases, breathing quickens, blood flows to muscles — preparing to fight or flee
Insulin: after a sugary meal, insulin tells liver and muscle cells to absorb glucose from the blood
Type 1 diabetes: the immune system destroys insulin-producing cells — patient needs insulin injections for life

keyTerms.hormone: A chemical messenger carried in blood from a gland to target organs
keyTerms.insulin: Hormone from the pancreas that lowers blood glucose
keyTerms.adrenaline: Hormone from adrenal glands triggering the fight-or-flight response
keyTerms.diabetes: A condition where blood sugar regulation fails — Type 1 (no insulin) or Type 2 (insulin resistance)

quiz.question: Hormones travel through:
quiz.explanation: Hormones are chemical messengers transported in the bloodstream to target organs.

quiz.question: Insulin is produced by:
quiz.explanation: Beta cells in the pancreas produce insulin to regulate blood glucose.

quiz.question: The fight-or-flight hormone is:
quiz.explanation: Adrenaline prepares the body for danger: faster heart, more blood to muscles.

quiz.question: Type 1 diabetes means:
quiz.explanation: In Type 1, the immune system destroys insulin-producing cells — lifelong injections needed.

quiz.question: Compared to the nervous system, hormones are:
quiz.explanation: Nervous = fast, short, electrical. Endocrine = slower, longer-lasting, chemical.

lessons.title: Ecosystems and Food Chains
lessons.content: An ecosystem includes all organisms and their physical environment. Producers (plants) make food via photosynthesis. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat plants. Secondary consumers eat herbivores. Tertiary consumers eat other carnivores. Decomposers break down dead matter. Only ~10% of energy transfers between levels. Food webs show interconnected chains.
examples: Pond: algae → tadpole → fish → heron
Removing foxes: rabbits overpopulate → overgraze → plants decline
Fewer top predators because 90% of energy is lost at each level

keyTerms.producer: Organism making its own food (plants, algae)
keyTerms.consumer: Organism eating other organisms for energy
keyTerms.decomposer: Organism breaking down dead matter, recycling nutrients
keyTerms.trophic level: A feeding level in a food chain (producer, primary consumer, etc.)

quiz.question: Energy originally comes from:
quiz.explanation: Plants capture solar energy through photosynthesis.

quiz.question: Why fewer top predators?
options: Only 10% of energy transfers between levels
quiz.explanation: 90% lost at each level — less energy available for top predators.

quiz.question: Decomposers:
quiz.explanation: They break down dead organisms, returning nutrients to the ecosystem.

quiz.question: A food web differs from a food chain because:
options: It shows multiple interconnected feeding relationships
quiz.explanation: Food webs show the complex reality — organisms eat multiple things.

quiz.question: Removing one species from a food web:
options: Affects many other species in the web
quiz.explanation: Interconnected relationships mean changes ripple through the entire ecosystem.

lessons.title: Adaptation and Natural Selection
lessons.content: Organisms have adaptations for survival. Structural: cactus spines reduce water loss. Behavioural: birds migrate. Physiological: camels tolerate high temperatures. Natural selection: individuals with beneficial traits survive more, reproduce, and pass traits on. Over generations, populations evolve. Evidence: fossils, DNA comparisons, homologous structures.
examples: Peppered moths: dark moths survived in polluted areas — natural selection
Arctic foxes: white fur in winter, brown in summer
Antibiotic-resistant bacteria: resistant individuals survive and multiply

keyTerms.natural selection: Survival and reproduction of best-adapted organisms
keyTerms.adaptation: A trait helping survival in an environment
keyTerms.evolution: Change in inherited characteristics over generations
keyTerms.variation: Differences between individuals of the same species

quiz.question: What drives natural selection?
options: Variation and survival of the fittest
quiz.explanation: Individuals with advantageous traits survive and pass those traits on.

quiz.question: Polar bear white fur is:
quiz.explanation: Physical features for survival = structural adaptation.

quiz.question: Antibiotic resistance shows:
quiz.explanation: Resistant bacteria survive antibiotics and reproduce — evolution in action.

quiz.question: Darwin's theory requires:
quiz.explanation: Natural selection needs: variation exists, competition for resources, beneficial traits are inherited, and changes accumulate over time.

quiz.question: Homologous structures (e.g., human arm and whale flipper) suggest:
quiz.explanation: Similar bone structures in different species point to a shared evolutionary ancestor.

lessons.title: Human Impact on Environment
lessons.content: Humans affect the environment through deforestation, burning fossil fuels (greenhouse gases → global warming), pollution (air, water, soil), and overexploitation. Global warming: rising sea levels, extreme weather, habitat loss. Conservation: protected areas, recycling, renewable energy, reforestation. Sustainable development meets current needs without compromising future generations.
examples: Amazon produces 20% of world's oxygen — deforestation threatens this
Plastic kills 100,000+ marine animals per year
Solar and wind produce energy without greenhouse emissions

keyTerms.biodiversity: Variety of living species in an ecosystem
keyTerms.sustainable development: Meeting present needs without harming future generations
keyTerms.deforestation: Large-scale removal of trees, destroying habitats and reducing CO₂ absorption

quiz.question: Main gas causing global warming:
quiz.explanation: CO₂ from burning fossil fuels is the primary greenhouse gas.

quiz.question: Deforestation contributes to climate change because:
quiz.explanation: Trees absorb CO₂ — removing them means more stays in the atmosphere.

quiz.question: A renewable energy source:
quiz.explanation: Solar is renewable — unlimited energy without emissions.

quiz.question: Biodiversity is important because:
options: Ecosystems are more stable with many species
quiz.explanation: Greater biodiversity = more resilient ecosystems, more resources, and better stability.

quiz.question: The greenhouse effect is:
options: Gases trapping heat in the atmosphere
quiz.explanation: Greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane) trap infrared radiation, warming the Earth.

lessons.title: Carbon and Water Cycles
lessons.content: The carbon cycle moves carbon through the environment. Carbon enters the atmosphere as CO₂ from respiration, combustion, and decomposition. Plants remove CO₂ through photosynthesis, converting it to glucose. Carbon passes through food chains when animals eat plants. Fossil fuels are carbon from ancient organisms — burning them releases stored carbon as CO₂. The oceans absorb CO₂ (forming carbonic acid — causing ocean acidification). The water cycle: evaporation (liquid → gas, driven by solar heat), condensation (gas → liquid, forming clouds), precipitation (rain, snow), collection (rivers, lakes, oceans), and infiltration (water soaking into the ground). These cycles are interconnected — disrupting one affects the other.
examples: Burning coal releases carbon stored for millions of years — adding 'new' CO₂ to the atmosphere
Deforestation removes carbon sinks — trees that would absorb CO₂ are gone
Rising ocean CO₂ absorption is causing acidification — threatening coral reefs and shellfish

keyTerms.carbon cycle: The continuous movement of carbon through atmosphere, organisms, oceans, and Earth
keyTerms.carbon sink: A reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases (forests, oceans)
keyTerms.water cycle: The continuous movement of water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection
keyTerms.ocean acidification: Oceans becoming more acidic as they absorb excess CO₂

quiz.question: Plants remove carbon from the atmosphere by:
options: Photosynthesis — absorbing CO₂ to make glucose
quiz.explanation: Photosynthesis takes CO₂ from the air and fixes it into organic molecules.

quiz.question: Fossil fuels are:
options: Carbon from ancient organisms stored over millions of years
quiz.explanation: Fossil fuels are compressed remains of ancient organisms — burning releases their stored carbon.

quiz.question: The water cycle is driven by:
quiz.explanation: The Sun's heat drives evaporation — the primary engine of the water cycle.

quiz.question: Ocean acidification is caused by:
quiz.explanation: CO₂ dissolves in seawater forming carbonic acid — lowering pH.

quiz.question: A carbon sink is:
options: Something that absorbs more carbon than it releases
quiz.explanation: Forests and oceans are major carbon sinks — they absorb and store carbon.

lessons.title: Biodiversity and Classification
lessons.content: Biodiversity is the variety of all living organisms on Earth. Classification organises organisms into groups based on shared characteristics. The hierarchy: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. The binomial system gives every species a two-part Latin name: genus + species (e.g., Homo sapiens). The five kingdoms: Animalia (animals), Plantae (plants), Fungi, Protista (single-celled eukaryotes), and Prokaryotae (bacteria). Modern classification also uses DNA analysis — species with more similar DNA are more closely related. Biodiversity is threatened by habitat destruction, pollution, climate change, overexploitation, and invasive species.
examples: Human classification: Animalia → Chordata → Mammalia → Primates → Hominidae → Homo → sapiens
A lion: Panthera leo. A tiger: Panthera tigris. Same genus (Panthera) means they're closely related
DNA shows humans and chimps share 98.7% of DNA — confirming very close evolutionary relationship

keyTerms.biodiversity: The variety of all living species in an area or on Earth
keyTerms.classification: Organising organisms into groups based on shared characteristics
keyTerms.binomial nomenclature: The two-part naming system: Genus species (e.g., Homo sapiens)
keyTerms.species: A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring

quiz.question: The correct order of classification hierarchy is:
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Kingdom, Species, Family, Class, Order, Phylum, Genus
Genus, Species, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family
quiz.explanation: King Philip Came Over For Good Spaghetti — a mnemonic for the hierarchy.

quiz.question: The binomial name for humans is:
quiz.explanation: Binomial = Genus (Homo) + species (sapiens). The genus is capitalised.

quiz.question: Two organisms in the same genus are:
quiz.explanation: Same genus = closely related. Same species = can interbreed.

quiz.question: Modern classification uses DNA because:
options: It reveals evolutionary relationships more accurately than physical features alone
quiz.explanation: DNA analysis reveals genetic similarity — a more objective measure of relatedness.

quiz.question: The biggest threat to biodiversity is:
quiz.explanation: Habitat loss (deforestation, urbanization) is the number one cause of species decline.

lessons.title: DNA and Genes
lessons.content: DNA is a double helix carrying genetic instructions. Four bases: A pairs with T, G pairs with C. A gene is a section of DNA coding for a protein. Humans have ~20,000 genes on 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total). The genome is the entire set of genetic material. DNA replication: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, complementary bases are added, producing two identical copies.
examples: Identical twins have the same DNA — that's why they look alike
A mutation in DNA can cause diseases like sickle cell anaemia
DNA fingerprinting uses unique patterns for forensic identification

keyTerms.DNA: Deoxyribonucleic acid — the molecule carrying genetic code
keyTerms.gene: A section of DNA coding for a specific protein
keyTerms.mutation: A change in DNA sequence that may alter the protein
keyTerms.genome: The complete set of genetic material in an organism

quiz.question: In DNA, adenine pairs with:
quiz.explanation: A-T and G-C are the base pairing rules.

quiz.question: Human body cells have:
quiz.explanation: 23 pairs = 46 chromosomes.

quiz.question: A gene codes for:
quiz.explanation: Genes contain instructions to build specific proteins.

quiz.question: DNA replication produces:
options: Two identical copies of the DNA
One copy and one different version
quiz.explanation: Each strand templates a new complementary strand — producing two identical double helices.

quiz.question: The human genome contains approximately:
quiz.explanation: Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes across 23 pairs of chromosomes.

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.content: Traits pass from parents through alleles (gene versions). Dominant (B) shows with one copy. Recessive (b) needs two copies. Homozygous = same alleles (BB or bb). Heterozygous = different (Bb). Punnett squares predict offspring. Bb × Bb = 25% BB, 50% Bb, 25% bb (3:1 phenotype ratio). Some traits are codominant or sex-linked (X chromosome).
examples: Brown eyes (B) dominant over blue (b) — Bb gives brown eyes
Two Bb parents can have a bb (blue-eyed) child — 25% chance
Colour blindness is X-linked recessive — more common in males

keyTerms.dominant: Allele showing its trait with just one copy
keyTerms.recessive: Allele only showing when two copies present

quiz.question: If both parents are Bb, fraction of bb offspring?
quiz.explanation: Punnett: BB, Bb, Bb, bb — one out of four is bb.

quiz.question: Heterozygous means:
quiz.explanation: Hetero = different. One dominant + one recessive.

quiz.question: Genotype vs phenotype:
quiz.explanation: Genotype is genetic makeup; phenotype is what you observe.

quiz.question: Why is colour blindness more common in males?
options: It's X-linked recessive — males have only one X
It's not more common in males
quiz.explanation: Males (XY) need only one copy of the recessive allele on their X. Females (XX) need two copies.

quiz.question: In a Punnett square, Bb × bb gives:
quiz.explanation: Bb × bb: Bb, Bb, bb, bb — 50% heterozygous, 50% homozygous recessive.

lessons.title: Evolution Evidence
lessons.content: Evidence for evolution: fossils show species change over time, comparative anatomy (homologous structures), embryology (similar early development), DNA comparisons (more similar = more related), and observed evolution (antibiotic-resistant bacteria). All life shares common ancestors. Speciation occurs when populations become so different they can't interbreed — often caused by geographical isolation.
examples: Horse fossils show gradual change over millions of years
Humans and chimps share 98.7% DNA
Darwin's finches: different beak shapes evolved for different food sources

keyTerms.speciation: Formation of new species through evolutionary divergence
keyTerms.natural selection: The mechanism driving evolution — survival of the fittest

quiz.question: Human arm and whale flipper similarity suggests:
quiz.explanation: Homologous structures indicate shared evolutionary ancestry.

quiz.question: Most direct evidence for evolution:
quiz.explanation: Fossils show how organisms changed over millions of years.

quiz.question: 98.7% shared DNA with chimps means:
quiz.explanation: High similarity = recent common ancestor.

quiz.question: Speciation requires:
quiz.explanation: When populations can't interbreed (e.g., separated by geography), they diverge into separate species.

quiz.question: Bacteria developing antibiotic resistance is:
quiz.explanation: Resistant bacteria survive, reproduce, and pass resistance on — natural selection in action.

lessons.title: Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology
lessons.content: Genetic engineering involves modifying an organism's DNA. Genes can be cut using restriction enzymes, inserted into vectors (e.g., plasmids), and transferred into other organisms. Applications: GM crops (pest-resistant, drought-tolerant, higher yield), medical insulin (human insulin gene inserted into bacteria that produce it), gene therapy (replacing faulty genes to treat genetic diseases), and forensic DNA profiling. GM crops are controversial: benefits include feeding growing populations with less pesticide; concerns include unknown long-term effects, corporate control of seeds, and impact on biodiversity. CRISPR-Cas9 is a revolutionary gene-editing tool — precise, cheap, and fast.
examples: Golden Rice: engineered to produce vitamin A — could prevent blindness in developing countries
Insulin: before genetic engineering, insulin came from pig and cow pancreases — now bacteria produce human insulin
CRISPR: scientists edited mosquito genes to reduce malaria transmission — a potential game-changer for Africa

keyTerms.genetic engineering: Modifying an organism's DNA by adding, removing, or changing genes
keyTerms.GM crop: A genetically modified crop with DNA altered for desired traits
keyTerms.CRISPR: A precise gene-editing tool that can cut and modify DNA at specific locations
keyTerms.gene therapy: Treating genetic diseases by replacing or repairing faulty genes

quiz.question: Genetic engineering uses restriction enzymes to:
quiz.explanation: Restriction enzymes are molecular scissors — they cut DNA at precise recognition sequences.

quiz.question: Human insulin is now produced by:
quiz.explanation: The human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria, which produce insulin in large quantities.

quiz.question: A concern about GM crops is:
options: Unknown long-term effects on environment and health
quiz.explanation: While GM crops offer benefits, potential risks to biodiversity and health need careful study.

quiz.question: CRISPR-Cas9 is:
quiz.explanation: CRISPR allows scientists to edit genes with unprecedented precision and affordability.

quiz.question: Gene therapy aims to:
options: Treat genetic diseases by fixing faulty genes
quiz.explanation: Gene therapy replaces or repairs defective genes — potentially curing inherited conditions.

lessons.title: Microorganisms and Disease
lessons.content: Microorganisms (microbes) include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protists. Most are harmless or beneficial — gut bacteria aid digestion, yeast makes bread rise, decomposers recycle nutrients. Pathogens are microbes that cause disease. Bacteria cause TB, cholera, food poisoning. Viruses cause flu, HIV, COVID-19. Fungi cause athlete's foot, ringworm. Protists cause malaria. The body defends against pathogens: skin (physical barrier), mucus (traps microbes), white blood cells (engulf pathogens, produce antibodies, produce antitoxins). Vaccination introduces weakened/dead pathogens to trigger immune memory — if the real pathogen invades later, the immune response is fast and strong.
examples: Antibiotics kill bacteria but NOT viruses — that's why they don't work for colds and flu
Vaccination: your body makes antibodies against measles without getting sick — protected for life
Malaria is spread by mosquitoes carrying the Plasmodium protist — killing millions in tropical regions

keyTerms.pathogen: A microorganism that causes disease (bacteria, virus, fungus, protist)
keyTerms.antibody: A protein produced by white blood cells that targets a specific pathogen
keyTerms.vaccination: Introducing weakened/dead pathogens to stimulate immune memory
keyTerms.antibiotic: A medicine that kills bacteria but not viruses

quiz.question: Antibiotics work against:
quiz.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria — they have NO effect on viruses.

quiz.question: Vaccination works by:
options: Stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells
Killing all bacteria in the body
quiz.explanation: Vaccines trigger immune memory — the body responds quickly if the real pathogen appears.

quiz.question: Which disease is caused by a virus?
quiz.explanation: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2 virus. Cholera = bacteria, athlete's foot = fungus, malaria = protist.

quiz.question: The first line of defence against pathogens is:
quiz.explanation: Skin keeps pathogens out; mucus traps them in airways and the gut.

quiz.question: Antibiotic resistance is a growing problem because:
options: Overuse of antibiotics selects for resistant bacteria
quiz.explanation: Misusing antibiotics kills susceptible bacteria but resistant ones survive and multiply.
